explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, Appendix A, says the environment part of the risk assessment should ask whether the remote pilot, and other aircraft in the area, will be able to see the anti-collision light for at least 3 statute miles considering weather and terrain such as fog, hills, and structures, and whether the flash rate is sufficient to avoid a collision. The light exists so other aircraft can see the drone, not only the pilot. Paragraph 5.7.2 says the pilot may rely on the manufacturer's statement but remains responsible for verifying it at the operating location. The pilot may reduce the light's intensity but may never extinguish it at night (107.29(a)(2)).
explanation.keyTakeaway: At night, ask whether terrain and weather will hide your light from other aircraft.

stem: The FAA rescinds the declaration of compliance for a drone model the pilot has been using for Category 2 operations. What does this mean for the pilot?

choices.text: It stays eligible as long as its Category 2 label is attached
It stays eligible because it was bought before the rescission
It is not eligible for Category 2 while the DOC is rescinded

explanation.correct: It is not eligible for Category 2 while the DOC is rescinded.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.160(d)(1) says no person may operate a small unmanned aircraft identified on a rescinded declaration of compliance while that declaration is rescinded. AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.10.1.1, says a rescission does not make the aircraft inoperable, but makes it ineligible for operations over people, so it can still fly ordinary Part 107 operations that do not go over people. Paragraph 8.10.3.3 says the FAA posts rescissions on its website. The label and the purchase date do not restore eligibility.
explanation.keyTakeaway: A rescinded DOC ends Category 2 or 3 eligibility, whatever the label says.

stem: Near a non-towered airport, a remote pilot monitors the CTAF for 20 minutes and hears no calls. Can the pilot conclude that no manned aircraft are nearby?

choices.text: Yes; every aircraft near the airport must call on the CTAF
No; some aircraft have no radio, and some pilots do not announce
No; pilots must announce only within 1 mile of the field

explanation.correct: No; some aircraft have no radio, and some pilots do not announce.
explanation.reason: AIM 4-1-9 says there is no substitute for alertness near an airport without an operating control tower, because other aircraft may not have communication capability or their pilots may not communicate their presence or intentions. A silent frequency does not prove the sky is empty, so the remote pilot must keep scanning and yield right-of-way under 14 CFR 107.37. The AIM recommends monitoring and communicating from 10 miles out, not 1 mile, and even that is not guaranteed.
explanation.keyTakeaway: A quiet CTAF is not an empty sky. Keep looking.

stem: A remote pilot wants to monitor traffic at a non-towered airport near a job site. Where can the pilot find the airport's CTAF?

choices.text: In the Chart Supplement, or by contacting any FSS
It is 122.9 at every airport, so no lookup is needed
Only by calling the airport manager on the phone

explanation.correct: In the Chart Supplement, or by contacting any FSS.
explanation.reason: AIM 4-1-9 says the CTAF for a particular airport is contained in the Chart Supplement and other aeronautical publications and can be obtained by contacting any FSS, and the FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide shows the CTAF in the sectional's airport data block. The CTAF may be a UNICOM, MULTICOM, FSS, or tower frequency. MULTICOM 122.9 is used only where there is no tower, FSS, or UNICOM.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Look up the CTAF. It is not the same frequency everywhere.

stem: A remote pilot is working 2 miles south of runway 36 at a non-towered airport. On the CTAF, a pilot reports 8 miles south, straight-in for runway 36. What should the remote pilot expect?

choices.text: The airplane entering a left downwind west of the runway
The airplane descending along the extended centerline from the south
The airplane flying over at least 1,000 feet AGL to circle

explanation.correct: The airplane descending along the extended centerline from the south.
explanation.reason: AIM 4-1-9 says a pilot making a straight-in approach without entering the traffic pattern should self-announce about 8 to 10 miles out. Runway 36 lands toward the north, so a straight-in arrival comes from the south along the extended runway centerline, descending, which puts it near the job site. It will not fly a downwind or overfly at pattern altitude. The remote pilot must yield under 14 CFR 107.37.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Straight-in for runway 36 means low traffic on the extended centerline south of the field.

stem: A job site is inside the Class E surface area of a non-towered airport. The remote pilot plans to call the airport's UNICOM on the radio and ask permission to fly. Does that meet Part 107?

choices.text: No; it needs prior ATC authorization, which UNICOM cannot give
Yes; UNICOM permission satisfies the authorization rule
No; the pilot needs written permission from the airport manager

explanation.correct: No; it needs prior ATC authorization, which UNICOM cannot give.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.41 requires prior authorization from Air Traffic Control to operate within the lateral boundaries of a Class E surface area designated for an airport, and AIM 11-1-2 says Part 107 operators request it through LAANC or DroneZone. AIM 4-1-9 says UNICOM is a nongovernment station that may provide airport information on request, so it cannot grant an ATC authorization. Part 107 has no requirement for an airport manager's written permission.
explanation.keyTakeaway: UNICOM is not ATC. Class E surface areas need a real authorization (LAANC or DroneZone).

stem: Near a hospital, a remote pilot hears a helicopter call itself 'MEDEVAC' followed by its call sign. What does this tell the remote pilot?

choices.text: It is a military helicopter on a training mission
It is an air taxi flight without an authorized call sign
It is an urgent medical flight that gets ATC priority

explanation.correct: It is an urgent medical flight that gets ATC priority.
explanation.reason: AIM 4-2-4 says the term MEDEVAC is used only for missions of an urgent medical nature and gives the flight priority handling by ATC. Air taxi operators without FAA authorized call signs use the prefix 'Tango.' Military aircraft use their own call sign systems. A remote pilot hearing MEDEVAC should clear the area early, since 14 CFR 107.37 requires yielding to all aircraft.
explanation.keyTakeaway: MEDEVAC = urgent medical flight with priority. Get out of its way early.

stem: Monitoring the tower frequency, a remote pilot hears the controller tell an airplane to 'enter a right downwind runway three zero.' Where will the airplane fly?

choices.text: Southwest of the runway, flying southeast, parallel to it
Northeast of the runway, flying northwest, parallel to it
Northeast of the runway, flying southeast, parallel to it

explanation.correct: Northeast of the runway, flying southeast, parallel to it.
explanation.reason: AIM 4-3-2 says the downwind leg is a flight path parallel to the landing runway in the opposite direction of landing. Runway 30 lands toward about 300 degrees, so downwind is flown toward about 120 degrees (southeast). In a right-hand pattern all turns are to the right, which puts the downwind leg on the right side of the landing direction, to the northeast of the runway. Flying northwest would be the landing direction, not downwind.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Downwind is opposite the landing direction. Right traffic puts it on the right side of the runway.

stem: During a job near an airport, a remote pilot notices large yellow crosses painted at each end of one runway. What do they mean?

choices.text: The runway is reserved for helicopter landings
The runway is closed, at least temporarily
The runway has right-hand traffic in effect

explanation.correct: The runway is closed, at least temporarily.
explanation.reason: AIM 2-3-6 says yellow crosses placed only at each end of a runway indicate that it is temporarily closed, and that permanently closed runways have yellow crosses at each end and at 1,000-foot intervals. Helicopter landing areas and right-hand traffic are marked or published differently. The remote pilot should not assume the other runways are quiet.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Yellow X on a runway = closed.

stem: A drone works just beyond the departure end of runway 27 at a non-towered airport, outside any authorization requirement. What does the AIM say departing airplanes normally do there?

choices.text: Turn left immediately after liftoff to stay inside the pattern
Level off at 400 feet AGL until they are beyond the airport
Climb straight out along the runway centerline past the runway end

explanation.correct: Climb straight out along the runway centerline past the runway end.
explanation.reason: AIM 4-3-2 says the departure leg begins after takeoff and continues straight ahead along the extended runway centerline, climbing until at least 1/2 mile beyond the departure end of the runway and within 300 feet of pattern altitude. AIM 4-3-3 says aircraft remaining in the pattern turn crosswind beyond the departure end. Departing traffic therefore climbs right over the area past the runway end, which 14 CFR 107.43 requires the drone not to interfere with.
explanation.keyTakeaway: The area past the departure end is directly under climbing traffic.

stem: An airport data block on a sectional chart reads CT - 118.3, followed by a star and a C in a circle. What does this tell the remote pilot?

choices.text: The tower is part-time, and 118.3 is the CTAF when it is closed
The tower is full-time, and Class C airspace surrounds it
The tower is part-time, and the CTAF is 122.9 when it closes

explanation.correct: The tower is part-time, and 118.3 is the CTAF when it is closed.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says CT gives the control tower's primary frequency, a star indicates part-time operation (with hours in the tower frequency tabulation), and the C symbol follows the Common Traffic Advisory Frequency. Here the C follows 118.3, so pilots self-announce on 118.3 when the tower is closed. The C does not mean Class C airspace, and AIM 4-1-9 says MULTICOM 122.9 is used where there is no tower, FSS, or UNICOM station on the airport.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Star = part-time tower. Circled C marks the CTAF.

stem: A sectional chart's airport data block shows 45 after the field elevation and lighting code. What does the 45 mean?

choices.text: The longest runway is aligned on a heading of 045 degrees
The longest runway there is about 4,500 feet long
The traffic pattern altitude is 4,500 feet MSL at this airport

explanation.correct: The longest runway there is about 4,500 feet long.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says the number in the airport data block is the length of the longest runway in hundreds of feet, and that usable length may be less. 45 therefore means about 4,500 feet. Runway headings appear in runway numbers, and pattern altitudes are published in the Chart Supplement, not in that position of the data block.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Data block runway length is in hundreds of feet: 45 = 4,500 feet.

stem: A remote pilot knows the AIM's standard pattern altitude of 1,000 feet AGL for propeller airplanes and wants to know whether a nearby airport uses something different. Where should the pilot look?

choices.text: The Chart Supplement entry for that airport
Nowhere; every airport uses exactly 1,000 feet AGL
The maximum elevation figure on the sectional

explanation.correct: The Chart Supplement entry for that airport.
explanation.reason: AIM 4-3-3 says the recommended pattern entry altitudes, such as 1,000 feet AGL for propeller-driven aircraft, should be maintained unless another traffic pattern altitude is published in the Chart Supplement. A maximum elevation figure shows terrain and obstruction heights in a chart quadrangle, not pattern altitudes. Knowing the real pattern altitude helps the remote pilot avoid interfering with traffic under 14 CFR 107.43.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Nonstandard pattern altitudes are published in the Chart Supplement.

stem: A remote pilot will film near an accident scene. During planning, the pilot realizes an EMS helicopter may need the same open area chosen for takeoff and landing. What does AC 107-2A's example suggest?

choices.text: Keep the one landing site, since the helicopter must wait for the drone
Skip planning, since emergencies cannot be anticipated before flight
Plan an alternate landing site and a safe spot to ditch the drone

explanation.correct: Plan an alternate landing site and a safe spot to ditch the drone.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, Appendix A, paragraph A.4.8.1, uses this exact situation: an EMS helicopter needs the planned landing area while the drone is low on power. Considering it before flight, the remote pilot might reach an acceptable level of risk by having an alternate landing site and possibly additional sites where the drone can be sacrificed to avoid risk to people or manned aircraft. Manned aircraft have right-of-way under 14 CFR 107.37, and the AC's point is that emergencies can be planned for.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Plan your outs before flight: an alternate landing site and a safe place to ditch.

stem: A remote pilot's charger has no automatic shutoff, and the pilot plans to leave batteries on it unattended overnight. What risk does the FAA's lithium battery guidance describe?

choices.text: Overcharging can make a lithium battery self-ignite
None, because lithium batteries stop charging when full
Only a shorter battery life, with no risk of fire

explanation.correct: Overcharging can make a lithium battery self-ignite.
explanation.reason: SAFO 10017 says FAA testing showed lithium-ion cells are capable of self-ignition, which can occur when a battery short circuits, is overcharged, is heated to extreme temperatures, is mishandled, or is defective, and that overheating can lead to thermal runaway. AC 107-2A, paragraph B.5, also lists improper charging as a cause of lithium battery fires. Following the manufacturer's charging recommendations, as AC 107-2A advises, helps prevent it.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Overcharging can ignite a lithium battery. Follow the manufacturer's charging guidance.

stem: Between flights, a crew member drops spare drone batteries loose into a toolbox with wrenches and screws. What is the hazard, according to FAA guidance?

choices.text: None, because the batteries are not being charged
Only scratches to the battery's outer case
Metal tools can short the terminals and start a fire

explanation.correct: Metal tools can short the terminals and start a fire.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph B.5, says lithium battery fires can be caused when a battery short-circuits or is mishandled. SAFO 15010 says spare lithium batteries should be individually protected to prevent short circuits, for example by taping exposed terminals or using separate bags, and must not come in contact with metal objects such as coins or keys. SAFO 15010 is written for airline baggage, but the short-circuit hazard it addresses is the same in a drone crew's toolbox. A battery does not need to be charging to short-circuit.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Keep spare batteries' terminals covered and away from metal.

stem: After the crew puts out a burning drone battery, it flares up again a minute later. What does SAFO 09013 say explains this?

choices.text: Heat from one cell drove nearby cells into thermal runaway
Water from the extinguisher reacted with the lithium
The battery recharged itself from the drone's motors

explanation.correct: Heat from one cell drove nearby cells into thermal runaway.
explanation.reason: SAFO 09013 says that once one cell in a battery pack goes into thermal runaway, it produces enough heat to drive adjacent cells into thermal runaway, and the resulting fire can flare repeatedly as each cell ruptures. That is why it recommends cooling the device with water after the fire is out. It lists water extinguishers as acceptable, so the water did not cause the flare-up, and a battery does not recharge itself from a stopped drone.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Battery fires can reignite cell by cell. After putting it out, keep cooling it.

stem: During a flight, the drone responds to stick inputs with a noticeable delay. What does AC 107-2A, Appendix C, recommend?

choices.text: Keep flying, but stay closer to the control station from now on
Discontinue flight until the control link is inspected and tested
Switch to manual mode and finish the job quickly

explanation.correct: Discontinue flight until the control link is inspected and tested.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, Appendix C, item 8, says that when control inputs are not synchronized or are delayed, the operator should discontinue flight or avoid further flight until the control link between the ground control unit and the aircraft is inspected and tested, and ensure reliable control communications before further flight, to prevent a possible loss of control resulting in a collision or flyaway. Flying on, closer or in a different mode, ignores that warning sign.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Delayed control response is a warning of lost control or flyaway. Land and fix the link.

stem: During an automated mapping mission, the drone loses its control link with the control station. According to AC 107-2A, what would the aircraft generally do?

choices.text: Keep flying the programmed mission or return home to land
Stop its motors immediately and fall to the ground below
Hover in place until the battery runs completely flat

explanation.correct: Keep flying the programmed mission or return home to land.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.2.3, says that during automated flight, control inputs come from components on board the aircraft, and if the remote PIC loses the control link, the aircraft would continue to fly the programmed mission or return home to land. Paragraph 5.2.3.1 says the remote PIC must still retain the ability to direct the aircraft, so the remote PIC should know which the aircraft will do.
explanation.keyTakeaway: On lost link, an automated mission keeps going or returns home. Know which your aircraft does.

stem: A remote pilot will inspect a house roof with a drone not eligible for flight over people. The residents are relaxing in the back yard. What does AC 107-2A suggest?

choices.text: Fly over them quickly, since brief passes over people are allowed
Ask them to stay indoors or under safe cover until the flight is done
Nothing, as long as the residents have agreed to have the drone fly

explanation.correct: Ask them to stay indoors or under safe cover until the flight is done.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.3, says that if the remote pilot selects a location where people are present, the pilot should have a plan to keep them clear of the operating area, and may direct people to remain indoors or under safe cover, such as a structure or stationary vehicle, until the flight has ended. Without a category of eligibility, 14 CFR 107.39 does not allow flight over people who are not directly participating, and agreeing to the flight does not make them participants.
explanation.keyTakeaway: If people are on site, have a plan to keep them clear: indoors or under safe cover.

stem: A drone not eligible for flight over people will fly a fast pass along a line 30 feet beside a group of spectators. What should the remote pilot consider, per AC 107-2A?

choices.text: Only whether its planned path crosses directly overhead
Its course and speed, but not what a failure would do
Its course, speed, and trajectory if a failure occurs

explanation.correct: Its course, speed, and trajectory if a failure occurs.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.3, says the remote pilot should consider risk mitigations and account for the small unmanned aircraft's course, speed, and trajectory, including the possibility of a failure, to determine whether it would go over a person. A fast pass beside a crowd could carry a failed drone over them even if the planned path never crosses overhead. Leaving out failure trajectories misses the AC's point: a failure at speed can carry the drone over people beside its path.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Plan for where a failed drone would go, not just where you intend it to go.

stem: For a night job, a remote pilot plans to use the same large operating area flown by day, relying on the anti-collision light and the telemetry screen. What does AC 107-2A say?

choices.text: The plan is fine, because the light alone shows where the drone is
Expect to shrink the area, since lights and telemetry cannot replace VLOS
Add a second anti-collision light and keep the same area

explanation.correct: Expect to shrink the area, since lights and telemetry cannot replace VLOS.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.9.3, says that in almost all night operations the remote PIC may need to restrict the operational area, because reduced lighting and contrast make it hard to see the aircraft's location, attitude, altitude, and direction of flight as 14 CFR 107.31 requires, and that a remote pilot cannot rely solely on the anti-collision lighting, telemetry displays, or both to comply with 107.31.
explanation.keyTakeaway: At night, plan a smaller area. The light and the screen do not satisfy VLOS by themselves.

stem: On a job, the visual observer will stand 600 feet from the remote pilot beside a noisy highway. When should the crew decide how they will communicate?

choices.text: Before the flight, for example by agreeing on handheld radios
During the flight, once a problem has actually come up
Never; the observer only watches and does not talk to the pilot

explanation.correct: Before the flight, for example by agreeing on handheld radios.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.9.2.2, says the remote PIC, person manipulating the controls, and VO must work out a method of effective communication that does not create a distraction and that the method must be determined prior to operation, and it allows communication-assisting devices such as handheld radios. 14 CFR 107.33 requires the crew to maintain effective communication, and the VO's job is to tell the pilot what they see.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Settle how the crew will talk before launch, especially over distance or noise.

stem: A remote PIC has listed the hazards of a job and judged how severe the risk of each one is. In AC 107-2A's basic hazard process, what comes next?

choices.text: Cancel the job, because any listed hazard rules out flight
Develop a plan to lessen each risk to an acceptable level
Fly the job, because listing hazards removes their risk

explanation.correct: Develop a plan to lessen each risk to an acceptable level.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, Appendix A, paragraph A.4.8.1, describes the basic hazard identification and mitigation process: consider the hazards of the particular operation, determine the risk severity, and then develop a plan to lessen (mitigate) the risk to an acceptable level. Identifying a hazard does not remove it, and a hazard does not automatically rule out the operation if it can be mitigated.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Identify, assess, then mitigate to an acceptable level.

stem: On a long job, a remote pilot has skipped breakfast and lunch and now feels lightheaded and shaky. Which IMSAFE item does this fail, and what should the pilot do?

choices.text: Illness; fly on, since hunger is not an illness
Eating; stop and eat before flying again
Alcohol; wait 8 hours before flying again

explanation.correct: Eating; stop and eat before flying again.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, Appendix A, paragraph A.4.8.2, lists the IMSAFE checklist, including Eating: am I sufficiently nourished? A pilot who is lightheaded from skipping meals is not fit to fly until the problem is fixed. 14 CFR 107.17 prohibits operating with a condition that would interfere with safe operation. Alcohol and the 8-hour rule in 107.27 do not apply here.
explanation.keyTakeaway: IMSAFE includes Eating. Hungry and shaky is not fit to fly.

stem: At night, a remote pilot uses off-center viewing to keep sight of the drone's dim light, but after a few seconds of holding the gaze the light fades again. What does the PHAK recommend?

choices.text: Stare straight at the light until it comes back into view
Use a bright flashlight to help the eyes refocus on the light
Shift the gaze to a new off-center point every 2 to 3 seconds

explanation.correct: Shift the gaze to a new off-center point every 2 to 3 seconds.
explanation.reason: The PHAK (FAA-H-8083-25C), Chapter 17, says that with off-center vision, images of an object viewed longer than 2 to 3 seconds disappear because the rods reach a photochemical equilibrium, so pilots should avoid viewing an object longer than that and shift the eyes from one off-center point to another. Looking directly puts the image in the night blind spot, and bright light destroys dark adaptation.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Off-center viewing works only if you keep shifting the gaze every 2 to 3 seconds.

stem: A remote pilot has finished the ground part of the preflight inspection and launched. Before starting the mission, what does AC 107-2A's preflight list suggest?

choices.text: Climb straight to 400 feet AGL to test the control link's range
Fly at a low controlled altitude and recheck all controls and stability
Start the mission and check controls on the first long flight leg

explanation.correct: Fly at a low controlled altitude and recheck all controls and stability.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 7.3.4, lists preflight inspection items, including starting the propellers to inspect for imbalance and, at a controlled low altitude, flying within range of any interference and rechecking all controls and stability. Climbing straight to 400 feet or checking controls mid-mission puts a possible problem far from the pilot and the ground. 14 CFR 107.49 requires the preflight check.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Finish preflight with a low hover and a controls check before going anywhere.

stem: A crack in a drone's motor mount was glued, but the operator cannot restore the part to its safe operational specification. What does AC 107-2A recommend?

choices.text: Fly it, but with lighter payloads, until the glue fails again
Replace the part with one that is in a condition for safe operation
Have someone sign off on the glued part, then fly it

explanation.correct: Replace the part with one that is in a condition for safe operation.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 7.2.3.1, says that if the operator or other maintenance personnel are unable to repair, modify, or overhaul a small UAS or component back to its safe operational specification, the operator should replace it with one that is in a condition for safe operation, and that all required maintenance should be completed before each flight. A sign-off does not restore a part to specification. 14 CFR 107.15 prohibits operating a small UAS that is not in a condition for safe operation.
explanation.keyTakeaway: If a part cannot be repaired to specification, replace it before flying.

stem: A drone model appears on the FAA's list of eligible aircraft with a declaration of compliance for Category 2 only. A remote pilot wants to use it for a Category 3 operation. Is it eligible?

choices.text: Yes; any model on the list may fly in any category over people
No; the FAA's list is only for Category 1 aircraft
No; eligibility is listed by category, and this is Category 2 only

explanation.correct: No; eligibility is listed by category, and this is Category 2 only.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraphs 8.10.3.2 and 8.10.3.3, say the remote pilot must determine whether the aircraft is listed on an FAA-accepted DOC appropriate to the category of the intended operation, and that the FAA website lists eligible aircraft by make, model, series, and category declared. A Category 2 declaration does not make the aircraft eligible for Category 3, which has its own requirements under 14 CFR 107.130. Category 1 aircraft need no declaration; the list covers aircraft declared for Categories 2 and 3.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Check both the model and the category on the FAA's eligibility list.

stem: A drone's manufacturer reports a possible safety issue with the model to the FAA. Does the report by itself make the model ineligible for operations over people?

choices.text: Yes; any reported issue rescinds the declaration at once
Not automatically, but all flights must stop for 30 days
Not automatically; the FAA first evaluates the report

explanation.correct: Not automatically; the FAA first evaluates the report.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 8.10.2.3, says reporting a safety issue to the FAA would not automatically mean that the FAA would determine the aircraft is no longer eligible to operate over people or that corrective action is necessary; the FAA would evaluate the report and work with the declaration holder. Rescission follows the process in 14 CFR 107.160. The remote pilot should still watch the FAA's list and check the aircraft's condition before each flight under 107.49. No automatic 30-day pause exists; the FAA evaluates the report and, if needed, follows the rescission process.
explanation.keyTakeaway: A safety report starts an FAA review. It is not a rescission by itself.
